(Today through next Wednesday)
WEATHER PATTERN OVERVIEW: Looking out my window, everything is
sadly brown again. After seeing anywhere from T to 7 inches of 
snow, most of the lower elevations, especially to the northern 
portions of the CWA, have seen most if not all of the snow melted 
during the daytime. This is the consistency we can begin to expect
during these next few weeks. As of right now, a weak ridge is 
currently entering the CWA. Simultaneously, with positive tilting
the associated HPC resides to the east of the ridge. This 
temporary ridge is going to provide us a very short break from the
precipitation, before it returns in the next system set to impact
the area beginning Wednesday night. Tonight, a deep inversion is 
expected to be complimented by the ridge for all but our most 
western forecast areas. This is expected to keep us relatively 
clear tonight, allowing most of the area to see lows in the teens 
and lower 20s, with the coldest temps being in the higher 
elevations. It is worth mentioning that ahead of this system, 
there is potential for some higher wind gusts, upwards of 25-40MPH
when looking in the mountain passes and higher elevated towns. 

We are expected to start seeing some weak shortwaves escape ahead
of the trough, which could bring some scattered rain/snow showers
to the northern portions of the CWA, but due to very very low 
CAPE values (<30), coverage is going to be minimal. In this 
system, moderate moisture advection is expected to bring us PWAT 
values elevated to around 0.2-0.5”, which may not sound like very 
high values to those from literally anywhere else, but it is a 
significant departure from standard climatological moisture 
values. As the larger scale system starts working its way into our
area, coverage of precipitation in general is expected to greatly
spike and become widespread. This transition is expected to occur
around the 18Z-00Z time frame for Humboldt, Lander, and far 
western Elko counties. This is expected to continue increasing 
coverage as we move into Wednesday night, and start seeing 
widespread snow showers. As of right now, snow totals are expected
to remain from trace to just below 1” for most of the lower 
elevations, upwards of 2-5” in the middle elevations, and upwards 
of 6”+ on the higher elevations in the CWA. What will make this 
more difficult to determine is both how long the system resides 
over our area, and the very finicky snow level. As of right now 
the average snow level for Wednesday daytime is looking to be 
around 5500’ give or take 200’. This makes it very difficult as 
this is where many high population towns in this region sit 
height-wise. What challenges the forecast is going to be how fast
our temperatures drop ahead of the system. As of right now, highs
for Wednesday are expected to sit in the upper 30s and lower 40s.
The forecast is expecting generally weak CAA ahead of the 
precipitation as the systems axis changes winds overhead from SW
to westerly. If wind speeds are stronger, CAA will be limited, 
causing us to see slightly less radiative cooling in the early 
night hours, so an initial precip type of rain can be expected. If
winds drop to the low end of the forecast, both radiative cooling
in the early night hours, and the CAA in the forward portions of 
the system will have the potential to skip the mixed precipitation
phase, and jump straight to snow.


This pattern is expected to spill over into the daytime hours of 
Friday with very cold temperatures in mind. Widespread synoptic 
lift will offer the best chances of deep snowfall in central 
Nevada, with storm total snowfall totals for the entire event 
reaching upwards of 2-5” in the valleys, and even higher amounts 
possible in the higher elevations and in the mountain passes. For 
these reasons, Winter Weather Advisories are possible. The real 
question that still needs addressed is “will my winter wonderland 
survive?” The short answer is “maybe.” The key will be mostly in 
the deeper portions of the valleys, but it still pertains to a 
majority of the CWA. In terms of any snow Thursday night into 
Friday morning sticking around long term is going to be based 
solely on how warm it gets, given total sunshine amounts remain 
somewhat low for Friday as the rest of the snow/rain continues to
fall. The issue is once again going back to the temperatures. 
During the day Friday, highs are expected to sit in the mid 30s to
upper 40s. So the best hope here is for those who still see 
precipitation when the temperatures peak right above freezing to 
still see some latent cooling as the top of the snow layer melts. 
As the next ridge begins to take its place on Saturday, we will 
see some of the coolest temperatures of the season so far. With
